displayQuote: What we do in life echoes in eternity

meta.title: Who really said "What we do in life echoes in eternity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Meditations — it is a line from Ridley Scott's Gladiator (2000), spoken by Maximus and used as the film's tagline. Written by the credited screenwriters David Franzoni, John Logan and William Nicholson, and still in copyright.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What we do in life echoes in eternity'?
meta.ogDescription: Marcus Aurelius never wrote it. Maximus says it in Gladiator (2000) — a modern, in-copyright screenplay wearing a Roman name, which inverts the usual rights assumption.

answer.label: A screenwriter — Gladiator (2000), not the Meditations
answer.authorDates: American screenwriter and playwright · co-credited on Gladiator (2000)
answer.sourceLine: It is a film line. Maximus says it in the opening minutes of Ridley Scott’s Gladiator (2000), rallying the legions in Germania, and it was used as the film’s tagline. The screenplay is credited to David Franzoni, John Logan and William Nicholson; the line is generally credited to Logan, though on a three-writer rewrite individual lines are rarely documented. It is not in the Meditations, in any translation, and Marcus Aurelius — who is a character in the film — does not say it there either.

source.excerpt: Brothers, what we do in life echoes in eternity.
trail: The line is in the film and can be watched: Maximus addresses the cavalry in the opening sequence, telling his men not to fear death. It also served as the marketing tagline, which is a large part of why it detached from the film so easily the film's dialogue ↗.

The screenplay went through three credited writers: David Franzoni wrote the original story and first draft, John Logan was brought in to rewrite the first act, and William Nicholson came last to soften Maximus. Dialogue was still being written on set. Secondary accounts credit Logan with this line specifically; we flag that as reported rather than documented, because per-line credit on a rewrite of this kind almost never is how the script was written ↗.

On the other side of the test: the sentence does not appear in the Meditations. It is not in Long (1862), not in Casaubon (1634), and not in the modern translations. Marcus does write about oblivion and posterity — usually to say that being remembered is worthless — which is close to the opposite of this Meditations, Long ↗.
source.excerptNote: A line of modern screen dialogue, written to be shouted from a horse. It is a good line — which is exactly the problem. Put a Roman name on it and it stops sounding like a film and starts sounding like a source.

source.rightsNote: This is the case that inverts the usual assumption. People quote it freely because ‘Marcus Aurelius’ means ancient and ancient means free — but the actual text is a screenplay from 2000, owned by its studio and writers, and protected for decades to come. Quoting one sentence with attribution to the film is ordinary fair use and entirely normal; putting it on merchandise, in an advertisement, or in a product as though it were public-domain Stoicism is not. The genuine Marcus Aurelius is free; this is not Marcus Aurelius. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Marcus Aurelius
author.metaLine: 121–180 AD · Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, and a character in the film
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius is doubly exposed here. He is the most quoted Stoic in the world, so any grave Roman-sounding sentence drifts toward him — and he is also in Gladiator, played by Richard Harris, which means people who half-remember the film place the line in his mouth rather than Maximus’s. The irony is sharp: the real Marcus spends the Meditations insisting that posthumous fame is worthless, that those who remember you will shortly be dead themselves, and that the applause of eternity is noise. He would not have written this line, and on his own argument he would have distrusted it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A modern in-copyright text wearing a Roman name. That combination does more damage than an ordinary misquote, because it does not just get the author wrong — it gets the rights backwards.

items.why: The sentence appears in no translation of the Meditations: not Casaubon (1634), not Long (1862), not the modern ones. There is no book, no section number, no Greek behind it, because the original language is English and the year is 2000.

Maximus says it to the legions in the opening sequence, and the studio used it as the tagline. Credited writers: Franzoni, Logan, Nicholson. Logan is the name usually attached to this line; treat that as reported, not established the dialogue ↗.

items.who: In copyright until well into this century
items.why: Ancient attributions are usually a licence to reproduce. This one is the reverse: believing the credit tells you the text is free, when in fact it is a protected screenplay owned by a studio. The false attribution is what makes people careless with it.

items.scope: What Marcus actually thought about echoes
items.why: The Meditations returns repeatedly to the worthlessness of being remembered — those who praise you will die, and so will those who remember them. He uses oblivion as a comfort, not a threat. The film’s line is a promise of immortality; his book is a systematic refusal of one.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Marcus Aurelius: it is a line from Gladiator (2000), spoken by Maximus, written by the film’s credited screenwriters — and still in copyright the film ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a great piece of screenwriting doing exactly its job: eight words, spoken to frightened men on horseback, that make the next ten minutes of slaughter feel like it means something. Hans Zimmer’s score does the rest.

It travels because it sounds ancient, and it sounds ancient because the film taught two generations what a Roman sounds like. Once the film credit falls away, the sentence has nowhere to live except the most famous Roman book there is.
detailsBody: David Franzoni wrote the original story and the first screenplay draft.
John Logan was hired to rewrite, reworking much of the first act — and is the writer usually named for this line.
William Nicholson came last, developing Maximus’s inner life, his friendship with Juba, and the afterlife thread the line belongs to.
Dialogue continued to be rewritten during shooting, which is why per-line credit is rarely documented.
The film premiered on 1 May 2000 and opened in the US on 5 May 2000.
The sentence then left the film entirely, and has been circulating with a Roman signature ever since.
context.pull: Not a Roman sentence with a modern audience. A modern sentence with a Roman accent.
